Apple and other tech giants may have to make an annual lump-sum payment to the EU under a revised digital services tax plan.

The EU hopes that by revising its earlier proposal, it can raise revenue without angering the White House……

Disputes over the digital services tax among EU member states have been longstanding, with Apple's services including iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Creator Studio and others often cited as examples.

Critics point out that companies generate substantial revenue by selling subscription services to EU citizens, yet may not pay any tax on these earnings in Europe. There are also concerns that a digital tax could disproportionately hit European businesses, while some worry that levying additional taxes on US companies would invite threats of retaliation from the White House.

According to the Financial Times, the European Commission has now put forward a compromise proposal aimed at satisfying all parties — except, of course, companies like Apple, Google, and Meta that would have to pay the new tax.

Officials indicated that authorities in Brussels are considering modifying the existing proposal to require all companies operating in the EU and generating annual revenues exceeding €100 million to pay an annual lump-sum tax…… Officials believe that adjusting the thresholds and amounts under the Core proposal to cover only very large companies would both increase tax revenue collected from tech groups and address criticism within Europe that the Core proposal would hit numerous medium-sized European companies.

The revised proposal would not single out companies selling digital services, but would apply to all large enterprises. Since it was precisely the previous proposal that led the White House to threaten retaliatory tariffs, the EU is hoping the new version will not trigger another trade war with the United States.

The top-liked comment was posted by cubbuc

I'm not opposed to taxing big tech. But let's be clear — by now everyone has to admit that companies capable of growing big simply won't be born in Europe; and even if they were, our feeble regulators wouldn't be able to stop them from being acquired by American giants.

You can keep playing this childish cat-and-mouse game with American tech, but you'll only end up losing badly.

Or you could actually do the hard work and address what is clearly a structural and systemic problem on this continent.

The amount each company would have to pay has not yet been finalised. The plan is to agree on the principle among the twenty-seven EU member states before setting the tax rate.

9to5Mac Take

This mess was supposed to be resolved through a global deal brokered by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). That agreement would have ensured that companies worldwide would have to pay at least some tax in each of the countries where they operate, and it had Apple's support.

However, Donald Trump pulled the United States out of the deal, prompting calls for an EU-specific version. The idea that Trump wouldn't object to a revised proposal seems, to me, overly optimistic.
